analysis.one_liner: Gives every child a $1,000 savings account at birth, with annual deposits up to $2,000 for lower-income families.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced in February 2023 with 16 Democratic and Independent cosponsors, it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a government-run savings account for every child, seeded with $1,000 at birth. Each year until the child turns 18, the Treasury would add more, on a sliding scale: up to $2,000 a year for the poorest families, tapering to nothing for households above five times the poverty line. At 18, the money could be spent only on college or job training, buying a home, retirement savings after age 59½, or other investments the government approves as building long-term wealth. The money would be invested in U.S. Treasury bonds by a government board, similar to the retirement plan for federal employees, and the accounts would not count against a family's eligibility for benefits like student aid.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, and most of all children in lower-income families, who would receive the largest deposits. A child born to a family below the poverty line would get the maximum $1,000 plus $2,000 every year for 17 years, roughly $35,000 in deposits plus interest by age 18. Children born after 2007 could apply for accounts before turning 18. Because the money is tax-exempt and ignored when calculating eligibility for federal benefits like student aid, it would reach poor families without cutting other support they receive.

how_it_helps.text: Every child born after December 31, 2023 would automatically receive a $1,000 account at birth, and children born after December 31, 2007 could request an account before turning 18.

Annual deposits run on a sliding scale by family income: $2,000 per year for households below the poverty line, tapering to $250 for households between three and five times the poverty line, and nothing above that.
Families that do not file tax returns are treated as having income below the poverty line, so the poorest children get the maximum deposit by default.
At 18 the money can be used for higher education, career and technical school, buying a home, retirement savings after 59½, or other long-term wealth-building investments approved by regulation.
The accounts grow tax-free, are exempt from federal tax, and are disregarded in determining eligibility for any federal benefit, including student financial aid.

The fund is invested in U.S. Treasury securities and managed with the same fiduciary, auditing, and accountability rules as the federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan, with annual reports to Congress and to account holders.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. Deposits come from the general fund of the Treasury with no dedicated funding source, and the bill bars using payroll taxes, so the cost would be added to federal borrowing or general revenue. The initial $1,000 goes to every child regardless of family wealth, though yearly deposits phase out for higher incomes.

drawbacks.text: The bill has no dedicated funding source: deposits come from the Treasury's general fund, payroll taxes are explicitly barred, and the annual cost of seeding and topping up accounts for every child born each year would run into the tens of billions of dollars.
The initial $1,000 goes to every child, including those from wealthy households; only the yearly contributions are phased out above five times the poverty line.
The money can only be invested in U.S. Treasury bonds, so returns would be limited to government bond interest, historically lower than a diversified stock portfolio would earn over 18 years.
The money is locked up: nothing can be withdrawn before age 18, and then only for approved uses, so a family facing an emergency cannot touch it.
The first beneficiaries would not see the money until 2041 at the earliest, so the bill offers no help to today's adults struggling with wealth gaps.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a large, permanent new spending program aimed squarely at closing the racial and class wealth gap at its starting point: childhood. The design is careful in several ways — deposits are progressive, the accounts don't reduce other benefits, and management is modeled on a well-regarded government plan — but the main honest objections are its cost with no funding mechanism and the low-return, low-flexibility structure. Whether it is worth it depends on weighing a generational wealth-building program against tens of billions a year in new federal spending.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or voted on it, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill on February 15, 2023, joined by 16 cosponsors, all Democrats and Independents, including Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress — no hearings, no markup, no vote.
No Republican cosponsored the bill at any point.
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without ever reaching the Senate floor or the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Treasury and taxpayers avoided tens of billions in new annual spending, and the private savings and investment industry kept its current role managing children's savings; low-income children gained nothing, since no wealth-building program was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers and the savings industry, for now

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, all from one party; none was enough to move the bill out of committee.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, which sat in his committee from February 2023 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Offered no support; not a single Republican cosponsored the bill during the two years it was pending.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents and no Republican ever signed on; the bill stalled in a committee chaired by a member of the sponsoring party, so partisan support alone was not enough to get it a vote.

industries.industry: Asset managers and children's savings providers (e.g., 529 plan administrators)
industries.note: The bill routes children's savings through a government fund invested directly in Treasury securities, bypassing private account managers who collect fees on savings products like 529 college plans. A cheaper public alternative would have displaced part of that fee stream.
Account holders could spend the money on college or technical school tuition from age 18, adding a new source of payment for students at those institutions.
